props.title: Grand Hotel
props.initialSlug: Lives intersect dramatically at luxurious Berlin hotel

sections.content: **Grand Hotel** (1932) revolutionized ensemble storytelling in Hollywood, weaving multiple narrative threads through Berlin's most luxurious hotel. Director Edmund Goulding masterfully juggles an all-star cast including Greta Garbo (delivering her famous "I want to be alone" line), John Barrymore, and Joan Crawford. The film established the "hotel movie" template that influenced countless others, from **Plaza Suite** (1971) to **Four Rooms** (1995). Its innovative structure of interconnected stories laid groundwork for later classics like **Nashville** (1975) and **Short Cuts** (1993).

sections.content: The hotel-as-microcosm concept flourished after Grand Hotel's success. **The V.I.P.s** (1963) transported the formula to an airport terminal with Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton, while **California Suite** (1978) updated it for the 1970s with Neil Simon's wit. These films use their settings as pressure cookers where class differences collapse and strangers' lives intersect dramatically.

Contemporary filmmakers continue drawing from Grand Hotel's blueprint. **Four Rooms** (1995) gave it a postmodern spin with Tim Roth's bellhop connecting four directors' stories. **The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel** (2011) relocated the concept to India, focusing on British retirees. Even Wes Anderson's **The Grand Budapest Hotel** (2014) pays loving homage to the genre's foundations while adding his distinctive style. SUBHEAD: Impact on Character-Driven Ensemble Films

Grand Hotel's influence extends beyond hotel settings. Its technique of weaving multiple protagonists' stories influenced ensemble films like **Dinner at Eight** (1933) and later **Gosford Park** (2001). The film's innovative use of overlapping narratives and chance encounters became standard tools for directors tackling complex social tapestries, from Robert Altman's **Nashville** (1975) to Paul Thomas Anderson's **Magnolia** (1999).
